Аспекты пограничного медико-санитарного контроля в контексте заболеваемости оспой обезьян: oсновные положения

25 ноября 2024 г.
 | Технический отчет
Скачать (297,8 kB)

Обзор

Генеральный директор Всемирной организации здравоохранения (ВОЗ) объявил 14 августа 2024 г., что резкое увеличение числа случаев заболевания оспой обезьян в растущем числе стран Африки представляет собой, согласно определению Международных медико-санитарных правил (ММСП) (2005 г.) (1), чрезвычайную ситуацию в области общественного здравоохранения, имеющую международное значение.

Оспа обезьян — это инфекционное заболевание, вызываемое вирусом оспы обезьян (MPXV), которое передается от человека к человеку. Существует две клады MPXV: клада I встречается главным образом в Центральной Африке, а клада II — в Западной Африке. Вирус оспы обезьян, ранее известный как вызывающий в основном зоонозную инфекцию, распространялся через контакты с животными и лишь затем вызывал вспышки заболеваемости в семьях и сообществах. В мае 2022 г. произошла глобальная вспышка заболеваемости оспой обезьян, которая в итоге охватила более 100 стран во всех регионах ВОЗ. Эта вспышка была связана главным образом с новой субкладой MPXV, известной как субклада IIb, которая распространяется в основном через половые контакты между мужчинами, практикующими секс с мужчинами. Другую основную затронутую группу составляют работники секс-индустрии; инфицированию эпизодически подвергаются медико-санитарные работники или члены семей (2, 3).

Настоящие временные рекомендации были составлены с целью оказать помощь в осуществлении соответствующих постоянных и временных рекомендаций, выпущенных Генеральным директором согласно требованиям в отношении обеспечения основных возможностей и другим положениям ММСП (2005 г.).

language_versions.body_text: Consideraciones sobre la salud transfronteriza y los puntos de entrada en relación con la viruela símica (‎mpox)‎: orientaciones provisionales 25 de noviembre de 2024 | Informe técnico Descargar (223,4 kB) Visión de conjunto El 14 de agosto de 2024, el Director General de la Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) determinó que el recrudecimiento de la mpox en un número creciente de países en África constituía una nueva emergencia de salud pública de importancia internacional en virtud del Reglamento Sanitario Internacional (RSI) (2005) (1). La mpox es una enfermedad vírica causada por el virus de la viruela símica (MPXV) que se transmite de persona a persona. El MPXV tiene dos clados, I y II: el clado I se detecta históricamente en África Central y el clado II en África Occidental. Conocido por provocar principalmente infecciones zoonóticas, el virus se propagó por el contacto con animales y de ahí pasó a provocar brotes en familias y comunidades. En mayo de 2022 se desencadenó un brote mundial de mpox que finalmente llegó a más de 100 países en todas las Regiones de la OMS. Este brote estaba vinculado mayoritariamente a un nuevo subclado del MPXV conocido como IIb, que se propagó principalmente por contacto sexual entre hombres que tienen relaciones sexuales con hombres. También se han visto afectados otros grupos de población clave, como los trabajadores sexuales; o en ocasiones trabajadores de la salud o familias (2, 3). Las presentes orientaciones provisionales ofrecen asesoramiento para apoyar la aplicación de las recomendaciones permanentes y temporales formuladas por el Director General en consonancia con las capacidades requeridas y las disposiciones del RSI (2005). title: Implementing Taenia solium control programmes in countries: monitoring and evaluation framework

content.body_text: Implementing Taenia solium control programmes in countries: monitoring and evaluation framework 25 November 2024 | Publication Download (5 MB) Overview This document aims to provide best practice on monitoring and evaluation of Taenia solium, as part of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) effort to develop M&E guidance across the neglected tropical diseases (NTDs). T. solium has been included in WHO’s list of NTDs since 2010 and is featured in the NTD road map 2021–2030. T. solium control programmes are relatively new compared with other NTD programmes and, as a result, the information available is limited. This monitoring and evaluation framework is based on the best information and evidence available at this time, as well as on experience from other disease control programmes. It will be updated as learning evolves and new diagnostic tools become available. Infection with the parasite T. solium causes two diseases in humans: taeniasis (infection with the adult parasite) and cysticercosis (infection with the larval stage of the parasite). Progress to control these diseases in endemic countries has been slow as resources are scarce, and adequate diagnostics, control tools and knowledge are lacking. Recently, however, new tools and guidance have become available, including the donation of taenicidal medicines (praziquantel and niclosamide), the publication of the Pan American Health Organization/WHO Guideline for preventive chemotherapy for the control of Taenia solium taeniasis and WHO Guidelines on management of Taenia solium neurocysticercosis, the commercial availability of the TSOL18 pig vaccine (and its inclusion in the terrestrial manual of the World Organisation for Animal Health) and the use of the vaccine in conjunction with oxfendazole in pigs, as well as results from an increasing number of field studies evaluating control interventions. This document responds to the request of several countries that are ready to begin implementing T. solium control programmes in order to provide guidance on diagnostic tools for use in public health programmes, on opportunities for integration and on monitoring and evaluation. The methods used to develop this monitoring and evaluation framework. Objectives of this document The main objective of this document is to provide practical operational best practice on monitoring and evaluation to countries implementing T. solium public health control programmes in order to reduce the disease burden caused by the parasite. It is based on existing diagnostic methods. The specific objectives are: to suggest indicators to monitor progress globally and nationally; and to provide details on surveys for confirming endemicity (mapping) or for monitoring and evaluation of a T. solium public health programme. Overview

This document aims to provide best practice on monitoring and evaluation of Taenia solium, as part of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) effort to develop M&E guidance across the neglected tropical diseases (NTDs). T. solium has been included in WHO’s list of NTDs since 2010 and is featured in the NTD road map 2021–2030. T. solium control programmes are relatively new compared with other NTD programmes and, as a result, the information available is limited. This monitoring and evaluation framework is based on the best information and evidence available at this time, as well as on experience from other disease control programmes. It will be updated as learning evolves and new diagnostic tools become available.

Infection with the parasite T. solium causes two diseases in humans: taeniasis (infection with the adult parasite) and cysticercosis (infection with the larval stage of the parasite). Progress to control these diseases in endemic countries has been slow as resources are scarce, and adequate diagnostics, control tools and knowledge are lacking. Recently, however, new tools and guidance have become available, including the donation of taenicidal medicines (praziquantel and niclosamide), the publication of the Pan American Health Organization/WHO Guideline for preventive chemotherapy for the control of Taenia solium taeniasis and WHO Guidelines on management of Taenia solium neurocysticercosis, the commercial availability of the TSOL18 pig vaccine (and its inclusion in the terrestrial manual of the World Organisation for Animal Health) and the use of the vaccine in conjunction with oxfendazole in pigs, as well as results from an increasing number of field studies evaluating control interventions.

This document responds to the request of several countries that are ready to begin implementing T. solium control programmes in order to provide guidance on diagnostic tools for use in public health programmes, on opportunities for integration and on monitoring and evaluation. The methods used to develop this monitoring and evaluation framework.

Objectives of this document

The main objective of this document is to provide practical operational best practice on monitoring and evaluation to countries implementing T. solium public health control programmes in order to reduce the disease burden caused by the parasite. It is based on existing diagnostic methods.

The specific objectives are:

  • to suggest indicators to monitor progress globally and nationally; and
  • to provide details on surveys for confirming endemicity (mapping) or for monitoring and evaluation of a T. solium public health programme.

language_versions.body_text: Mise en œuvre des programmes de lutte contre Tænia solium dans les pays : cadre de suivi et d’évaluation 25 novembre 2024 | Publication Télécharger (2,5 MB) Vue d’ensemble Ce document vise à fournir des meilleures pratiques sur le suivi et l'évaluation de Taenia solium, dans le cadre des efforts de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) pour développer des orientations en matière de suivi et d'évaluation pour les maladies tropicales négligées (MTN). T. solium figure sur la liste des MTN de l'OMS depuis 2010 et est inclus dans la feuille de route des MTN 2021-2030. L'infection par le parasite T. solium provoque deux maladies chez l'homme : la téniase (infection par le parasite adulte) et la cysticercose (infection par le stade larvaire du parasite). Les progrès pour contrôler ces maladies dans les pays endémiques ont été lents, les ressources étant rares, et il manque des diagnostics, des outils de contrôle et des connaissances adéquates. Cependant, récemment, de nouveaux outils et des orientations sont devenus disponibles, notamment la donation de médicaments taenicides (praziquantel et niclosamide), la publication de la ligne directrice de l'Organisation panaméricaine de la santé/OMS pour la chimiothérapie préventive visant à contrôler la téniase à Taenia solium et les lignes directrices de l'OMS sur la gestion de la neurocysticercose à Taenia solium, la disponibilité commerciale du vaccin TSOL18 pour les porcs (et son inclusion dans le manuel terrestre de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé animale) et l'utilisation du vaccin en conjonction avec l'oxfendazole chez les porcs, ainsi que les résultats d'un nombre croissant d'études sur le terrain évaluant le contrôle des interventions. Ce document répond à la demande de plusieurs pays prêts à commencer à mettre en œuvre des programmes de contrôle de T. solium afin de fournir des orientations sur les outils diagnostiques à utiliser dans les programmes de santé publique, sur les opportunités d'intégration et sur le suivi et l'évaluation. Les méthodes utilisées pour développer ce cadre de suivi et d'évaluation. Objectifs de ce document : L'objectif principal de ce document est de fournir des meilleures pratiques opérationnelles concrètes sur le suivi et l'évaluation aux pays mettant en œuvre des programmes de contrôle de santé publique pour T. solium afin de réduire le fardeau de la maladie causé par le parasite. Il est basé sur les méthodes diagnostiques existantes. Les objectifs spécifiques sont : suggérer des indicateurs pour suivre les progrès à l'échelle mondiale et nationale ; et fournir des détails sur les enquêtes pour confirmer l'endémie (cartographie) ou pour le suivi et l'évaluation d'un programme de santé publique T. solium. language_versions.title: Implementación de programas de control de Taenia solium en los países: marco de monitoreo y evaluación
language_versions.body_text: Implementación de programas de control de Taenia solium en los países: marco de monitoreo y evaluación 25 de noviembre de 2024 | Publicación Descargar (3,6 MB) Visión de conjunto El presente documento tiene por objetivo presentar las mejores prácticas para el monitoreo y la evaluación de T. solium como parte de los esfuerzos de la OMS destinados a orientar el monitoreo y la evaluación de las ETD. T. solium fue incluida en la lista de ETD de la OMS en 2010 y figura en la hoja de ruta para las ETD 2021-2030. Los programas de control de T. solium son relativamente nuevos en comparación con otros programas de ETD, por lo que la información disponible es limitada. El presente marco de monitoreo y evaluación se basa en las mejores informaciones y evidencias disponibles en este momento, así como en la experiencia de los programas de control de otras enfermedades, y se actualizará a medida que evolucionen los conocimientos y se disponga de nuevas herramientas de diagnóstico. La infección por T. solium causa dos enfermedades en el ser humano: la teniasis (infección por el parásito adulto) y la cisticercosis (infección por el parásito en fase larvaria). Los avances en el control de estas enfermedades en los países endémicos han sido lentos, ya que los recursos son escasos y faltan herramientas de diagnóstico, herramientas de control y conocimientos suficientes. Sin embargo, recientemente han surgido nuevas herramientas, como la donación de medicamentos tenicidas (praziquantel y niclosamida) o la comercialización de la vacuna TSOL18 para cerdos (ya incluida en el Manual de las pruebas de diagnóstico y de las vacunas para los animales terrestres de la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal) y su uso junto con oxfendazol, y nuevas orientaciones, como la publicación de las directrices de la Organización Panamericana de la Salud/OMS sobre la quimioterapia preventiva para el control de la teniasis por T. solium y de las directrices de la OMS sobre el manejo de la neurocisticercosis por T. solium, además de los resultados de un número creciente de estudios de campo en los que se han evaluado las intervenciones de control. El presente documento responde a la petición hecha por varios países que están listos para empezar a implementar programas de control de T. solium para que se les proporcionen orientaciones sobre las herramientas de diagnóstico que se pueden utilizar en los programas de salud pública (6), sobre las oportunidades de integración y sobre el monitoreo y la evaluación. Los métodos utilizados para elaborar este marco de monitoreo y evaluación. El presente marco de monitoreo y evaluación se basa en las mejores informaciones y evidencias disponibles en este momento, así como en la experiencia de los programas de control de otras enfermedades, y se actualizará a medida que evolucionen los conocimientos y se disponga de nuevas herramientas de diagnóstico.

La infección por T. solium causa dos enfermedades en el ser humano: la teniasis (infección por el parásito adulto) y la cisticercosis (infección por el parásito en fase larvaria). Los avances en el control de estas enfermedades en los países endémicos han sido lentos, ya que los recursos son escasos y faltan herramientas de diagnóstico, herramientas de control y conocimientos suficientes. Sin embargo, recientemente han surgido nuevas herramientas, como la donación de medicamentos tenicidas (praziquantel y niclosamida) o la comercialización de la vacuna TSOL18 para cerdos (ya incluida en el Manual de las pruebas de diagnóstico y de las vacunas para los animales terrestres de la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal) y su uso junto con oxfendazol, y nuevas orientaciones, como la publicación de las directrices de la Organización Panamericana de la Salud/OMS sobre la quimioterapia preventiva para el control de la teniasis por T. solium y de las directrices de la OMS sobre el manejo de la neurocisticercosis por T. solium, además de los resultados de un número creciente de estudios de campo en los que se han evaluado las intervenciones de control.

El presente documento responde a la petición hecha por varios países que están listos para empezar a implementar programas de control de T. solium para que se les proporcionen orientaciones sobre las herramientas de diagnóstico que se pueden utilizar en los programas de salud pública (6), sobre las oportunidades de integración y sobre el monitoreo y la evaluación. Los métodos utilizados para elaborar este marco de monitoreo y evaluación.

content.body_text: Standards and recommendations for burns care in mass casualty incidents 25 November 2024 | Guideline Download (1.9 MB) Overview Caring for burns patients from the incident scene to definitive treatment can be a complex, resource-consuming process with the potential to overwhelm health system capacity. title: Considerations for wastewater and environmental surveillance for monkeypox virus: Interim guidance

content.body_text: Considerations for wastewater and environmental surveillance for monkeypox virus: Interim guidance 25 November 2024 | Technical document Download (511.2 kB) Overview Wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) has potential to provide actionable information as part of multimodal surveillance for mpox. Use cases are; early detection, as well as reassurance of the absence, of transmission to enable targeted risk communication and responses, differentiation of circulating virus clades subject to validation and optimization of clade specific laboratory methods, and quantification of trends particularly in sewered and moderate to high case load settings if research further validates consistent correlation with cases. Case-based surveillance for mpox remains the priority and any WES must be integrated as part of multimodal surveillance. Technical and operational feasibility of WES has been demonstrated in sewered settings and to a lesser extent in unsewered settings. Cost-efficiency may be optimized though integration with existing WES for other targets (e.g., polioviruses or SARS-CoV-2). Ethical and legal aspects should be considered, particularly for vulnerable or marginalized population groups. Further research is needed to outline best practice and develop recommendations on WES for mpox. content.body_html:
Considerations for wastewater and environmental surveillance for monkeypox virus: Interim guidance

25 November 2024
 | Technical document
Download (511.2 kB)

Overview

Wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) has potential to provide actionable information as part of multimodal surveillance for mpox. Use cases are; early detection, as well as reassurance of the absence, of transmission to enable targeted risk communication and responses, differentiation of circulating virus clades subject to validation and optimization of clade specific laboratory methods, and quantification of trends particularly in sewered and moderate to high case load settings if research further validates consistent correlation with cases.

Case-based surveillance for mpox remains the priority and any WES must be integrated as part of multimodal surveillance. Technical and operational feasibility of WES has been demonstrated in sewered settings and to a lesser extent in unsewered settings. Cost-efficiency may be optimized though integration with existing WES for other targets (e.g., polioviruses or SARS-CoV-2). Ethical and legal aspects should be considered, particularly for vulnerable or marginalized population groups. Further research is needed to outline best practice and develop recommendations on WES for mpox.

language_versions.title: Considérations relatives à la surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement pour la détection et le suivi du virus de l’orthopoxvirose simienne : orientations provisoires
language_versions.body_text: Considérations relatives à la surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement pour la détection et le suivi du virus de l’orthopoxvirose simienne : orientations provisoires 25 novembre 2024 | Rapport technique Télécharger (785,9 kB) Vue d’ensemble La surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement (ou WES, pour l’acronyme en anglais (wastewater and environmental surveillance)) peut fournir des informations exploitables dans le cadre de la surveillance multimodale de l’orthopoxvirose simienne. Les cas d’utilisation sont les suivants : détection précoce de la transmission, ainsi que l’assurance de l’absence de transmission; différenciation des clades de virus en circulation; quantification des tendances, en particulier dans les zones raccordées à des réseaux d’égouts et dans les zones où le nombre de cas est modéré à élevé. . La surveillance basée sur les cas relative à l’orthopoxvirose simienne reste la priorité et toute activité de WES complémentaire pour l’orthopoxvirus simien (MPXV) doit être intégrée dans le cadre de la surveillance multimodale. La faisabilité technique et opérationnelle de WES a été démontrée dans les environnements raccordés à des réseaux d’égouts et, dans une moindre mesure, dans les environnements dépourvus d’égouts. Le rapport coût-efficacité peut être optimisé grâce à l’intégration au sein d’activités existantes de surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement pour d’autres cibles (par exemple, les poliovirus ou le SARS-CoV-2). Les aspects éthiques et juridiques doivent être pris en compte, notamment en ce qui concerne les groupes de population vulnérables ou marginalisés. Des recherches supplémentaires sont nécessaires pour définir les bonnes pratiques et formuler des recommandations sur la surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement dans le cas de l’orthopoxvirose simienne. Vue d’ensemble

La surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement (ou WES, pour l’acronyme en anglais (wastewater and environmental surveillance)) peut fournir des informations exploitables dans le cadre de la surveillance multimodale de l’orthopoxvirose simienne. Les cas d’utilisation sont les suivants : détection précoce de la transmission, ainsi que l’assurance de l’absence de transmission; différenciation des clades de virus en circulation; quantification des tendances, en particulier dans les zones raccordées à des réseaux d’égouts et dans les zones où le nombre de cas est modéré à élevé..
La surveillance basée sur les cas relative à l’orthopoxvirose simienne reste la priorité et toute activité de WES complémentaire pour l’orthopoxvirus simien (MPXV) doit être intégrée dans le cadre de la surveillance multimodale. La faisabilité technique et opérationnelle de WES a été démontrée dans les environnements raccordés à des réseaux d’égouts et, dans une moindre mesure, dans les environnements dépourvus d’égouts. Le rapport coût-efficacité peut être optimisé grâce à l’intégration au sein d’activités existantes de surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement pour d’autres cibles (par exemple, les poliovirus ou le SARS-CoV-2). Les aspects éthiques et juridiques doivent être pris en compte, notamment en ce qui concerne les groupes de population vulnérables ou marginalisés. Des recherches supplémentaires sont nécessaires pour définir les bonnes pratiques
et formuler des recommandations sur la surveillance des eaux usées et de l’environnement dans le cas de l’orthopoxvirose simienne.

title: Progress on the proportion of domestic and industrial wastewater flows safely treated – Mid-term status of SDG Indicator 6.3.1 and acceleration needs, with a special focus on climate change, wastewater reuse and health

content.body_text: Progress on the proportion of domestic and industrial wastewater flows safely treated – Mid-term status of SDG Indicator 6.3.1 and acceleration needs, with a special focus on climate change, wastewater reuse and health 22 November 2024 | Technical document Download (9.7 MB) Overview This report presents the global status on wastewater treatment and acceleration needs to achieve target 6.3 by 2030, based on the latest data on indicator 6.3.1 (total wastewater flows as well as flows from industrial sources and households). Over the 107 countries reporting some wastewater statistics for 2022 (representing 73 per cent of the world’s population) in the present report, the proportion of total wastewater receiving some level of treatment (76 per cent) could only be calculated for 73 countries (representing 42 per cent of the global population); whereas the proportion of total wastewater “safely” (i.e. at least secondary treatment) treated (60 per cent) could only be calculated for 42 countries (representing 12 per cent of the population). These data are insufficient to establish global statistics. Reporting on industrial wastewater treatment remains limited, with data only reported from 22 countries representing 8 per cent of the global population. In these countries, only 38 per cent of industrial wastewater was reported as treated, and only 27 per cent was safely treated. Globally, in 2022 42% of household (domestic) wastewater was not safely treated before discharge, leading to an estimated 113 billion m3 of household wastewater being released to the environment with inadequate or no treatment. Much of the fraction of household wastewater that was not safely treated was attributable to households lacking adequate blackwater and greywater collection systems, such as sewer connections or septic tanks (45 per cent). WHO Team Water, Sanitation, Hygiene and Health (WSH) Editors World Health Organization, United Nations Human Settlements Programme Number of pages 101 Reference numbers ISBN: 978-92-4-009908-1 Copyright
content.body_html:
Progress on the proportion of domestic and industrial wastewater flows safely treated – Mid-term status of SDG Indicator 6.3.1 and acceleration needs, with a special focus on climate change, wastewater reuse and health

22 November 2024
 | Technical document
Download (9.7 MB)

Overview

This report presents the global status on wastewater treatment and acceleration needs to achieve target 6.3 by 2030, based on the latest data on indicator 6.3.1 (total wastewater flows as well as flows from industrial sources and households).

Over the 107 countries reporting some wastewater statistics for 2022 (representing 73 per cent of the world’s population) in the present report, the proportion of total wastewater receiving some level of treatment (76 per cent) could only be calculated for 73 countries (representing 42 per cent of the global population); whereas the proportion of total wastewater “safely” (i.e. at least secondary treatment) treated (60 per cent) could only be calculated for 42 countries (representing 12 per cent of the population). These data are insufficient to establish global statistics.

Reporting on industrial wastewater treatment remains limited, with data only reported from 22 countries representing 8 per cent of the global population. In these countries, only 38 per cent of industrial wastewater was reported as treated, and only 27 per cent was safely treated.

Globally, in 2022 42% of household (domestic) wastewater was not safely treated before discharge, leading to an estimated 113 billion m3 of household wastewater being released to the environment with inadequate or no treatment. Much of the fraction of household wastewater that was not safely treated was attributable to households lacking adequate blackwater and greywater collection systems, such as sewer connections or septic tanks (45 per cent).

content.body_text: Country cooperation strategy, Maldives: 2024–2029 CCS Maldives 21 November 2024 | Country Cooperation Strategy Download (4.5 MB) Overview The Country Cooperation Strategy (CCS) is framed around the WHO General Programme of Work (GPW), specifically GPW 13 and GPW 14, and the WHO South-East Asia Regional Director’s priorities and addresses the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. At the same time, it is anchored in the national development priorities and the United Nations Sustainable Development Assistance Framework (UNSDCF) that has been formulated to support countries on the road to progress with the SDGs. The current CCS builds on the recommendations of the final review of the CCS in 2018–2022. It identifies a set of agreed joint priorities for WHO collaboration, covering those areas where WHO has a comparative advantage in order to ensure public health impact. The strategic priorities for this CCS includes: 1. Addressing social, economic and commercial determinants of health 2. Investing in quality-assured primary health care 3. Addressing the unmet health needs of vulnerable groups 4. Strengthening health system performance 5. Building health system resilience towards emergencies and health threats. Country cooperation strategy, Maldives: 2024–2029

CCS Maldives

21 November 2024
 | Country Cooperation Strategy
Download (4.5 MB)

Overview

The Country Cooperation Strategy (CCS) is framed around the WHO General Programme of Work (GPW), specifically GPW 13 and GPW 14, and the WHO South-East Asia Regional Director’s priorities and addresses the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. At the same time, it is anchored in the national development priorities and the United Nations Sustainable Development Assistance Framework (UNSDCF) that has been formulated to support countries on the road to progress with the SDGs. The current CCS builds on the recommendations of the final review of the CCS in 2018–2022. It identifies a set of agreed joint priorities for WHO collaboration, covering those areas where WHO has a comparative advantage in order to ensure public health impact.

The strategic priorities for this CCS includes:

1.  Addressing social, economic and commercial determinants of health

2. Investing in quality-assured primary health care

3. Addressing the unmet health needs of vulnerable groups

4. Strengthening health system performance

5. Building health system resilience towards emergencies and health threats.

概述

《一切为了健康，人人享有健康》是世卫组织第三份投资论证，它与新的《工作总规划》（GPW14）一起制定，旨在倡导在2025-2028年期间为世卫组织提供充足的资金。

这份投资论证以GPW14的主题“实现健康、增进健康和维护健康”为视角，突出了关键政策承诺和可交付成果，并表明世卫组织将与会员国和合作伙伴合作，拯救另外4000万人的生命。

该投资论证是世卫组织投资回合的重要宣传文件，旨在从广泛的筹资基础上确保世卫组织获得灵活、可预测的资金。

title: Ninth Meeting of the WHO South-East Asia Regional Verification Commission for measles and rubella elimination

content.body_text: Ninth Meeting of the WHO South-East Asia Regional Verification Commission for measles and rubella elimination 23–25 September 2024 Kathmandu, Nepal, 2024 21 November 2024 | Meeting report Download (1001.8 kB) Overview The Regional Verification Commission (RVC) for measles and rubella elimination for the WHO South-East Asia Region was established by the Regional Director in March 2016 to verify progress towards measles and rubella elimination. The SEA-RVC meets annually to review progress made by Member States towards measles and rubella elimination based on annual progress report submitted by respective National Verification Committees. This report outlines the conclusions and the recommendations made by the SEA-RVC during its Ninth Annual Meeting in September 2024. The SEA-RVC concluded that while the target for 2023 has been missed, significant progress has been made towards measles and rubella elimination in the Region. The Commission also concluded and verified that measles elimination has been sustained in Bhutan, DPR Korea, Maldives and Timor-Leste and that rubella elimination has been sustained in Bhutan, DPR Korea, Maldives, Sri Lanka and Timor-Leste. The commission also confirmed that measles transmission has been re-established in Sri Lanka and classified Nepal as having eliminated rubella pending verification. The Commission categorized the remaining countries as endemic for measles and rubella transmission. WHO Team Immunization & Vaccines Development, SEARO Regional Office for the South East Asia (RGO), WHO South-East Asia Editors World Health Organization. content.body_html:
Multiple first-line therapies as part of the response to antimalarial drug resistance

An implementation guide

20 November 2024
 | Manual
Download (232.5 kB)

Overview

Effective malaria case management requires quick access to diagnostics and antimalarial treatments to reduce illness and death. Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) has been essential to malaria treatment since 2001, as it combines artemisinin for rapid parasite reduction with a partner drug to ensure complete cure. However, resistance to antimalarial drugs, where parasites survive standard doses, threatens malaria control.

Partial resistance to artemisinin, linked to Pfkelch13 mutations, has recently emerged in several African countries, leading to slower parasite clearance times. Artemisinin partial resistance does not lead to ACT failure where the partner medicines are still effective. However, additional resistance to partner drugs would jeopardize ACT effectiveness. To address this threat, WHO launched a strategy to respond to drug resistance in Africa in 2022. This strategy aims to improve detection, enable timely responses, and reduce resistance impact through evidence-based measures.

The strategy includes multiple measures, including one on multiple first-line therapies (MFT) which aims to extend the therapeutic lifespan of ACTs. This implementation guide provides guidance for malaria programmes by defining MFT, reviewing their impact on resistance, assessing implications for policy and implementation, and identifying evidence gaps for future research.

title: Report of the third Life Course Network meeting, 28-30 November 2023: Extending healthy ageing across the life course

content.body_text: Report of the third Life Course Network meeting, 28-30 November 2023: Extending healthy ageing across the life course Connecting healthy development and healthy ageing 20 November 2024 | Meeting report Download (5.2 MB) Overview World Health Organization (WHO)’s work on the life course – connecting healthy development and healthy ageing – aims to extend learning on healthy ageing and connect it to other efforts to improve people’s abilities and capacities, such as supports for early child development. This perspective considers the well-being of the whole person, not simply a focus on illness or disease. The third Life Course Network meeting followed two previous meetings in June and December 2022. The WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA) hosted a hybrid meeting in Geneva, 28–30 November 2023, with over 40 experts leading eight working groups of 200 individuals from life course research centres, other academics, policy-makers, civil society and representatives from the six WHO regional offices and other WHO staff, attending the meeting in person. Working groups and the MCA Life Course team prepared and discussed 18 project papers, including a draft WHO-wide framework on putting a life course approach into practice. The meeting comprised six sessions to take stock of progress and facilitate learning across working groups. title: Guidance for human genome data collection, access, use and sharing

content.body_text: Guidance for human genome data collection, access, use and sharing 20 November 2024 | Guidance (normative) Download (1.2 MB) Overview The ethical, legal, and equitable sharing of human genomic data is critical to advancing global health research and ensuring fair access to the benefits of genomics. The WHO’s new document outlines a comprehensive set of globally applicable principles designed to guide stakeholders in the responsible collection, use, and sharing of human genome data. This document serves as a key resource to navigate complex issues surrounding data governance, with the aim of fostering transparency, promoting equity, and safeguarding individual and collective rights. These principles are intended to support the implementation of best practices across diverse settings, thereby enhancing the global capacity for genomic research and its translation into health benefits for all. title: Accelerating optimal approval of priority formulations for antibiotic use in children: meetings report, 7 December 2023 and 19-20 March 2024

content.body_text: Accelerating optimal approval of priority formulations for antibiotic use in children: meetings report, 7 December 2023 and 19-20 March 2024 20 November 2024 | Meeting report Download (1.9 MB) Overview On 24 March 2023, WHO launched the first-ever list of priority paediatric formulations for antibiotics, addressing critical gaps in age-appropriate treatments for infants and children. This list, developed through WHO’s Paediatric Drug Optimization (PADO) process, identifies antibiotics urgently needing development to treat infections from high-priority pathogens. WHO, leveraging GAP-f and partners like GARDP and PENTA, led a technical consultation that concluded in March 2024 to review regulatory frameworks and streamline clinical research, aiming to accelerate regulatory approvals and ensure equitable access to effective treatments. The outcomes of this meeting are captured in this report, underscoring the collaborative efforts needed to advance essential paediatric formulations, minimize delays, and support globally aligned, evidence-based care for serious infections in children. WHO Team GAP-F Editors World Health Organization Number of pages 24 Reference numbers ISBN: 9789240103351 Copyright
content.body_html:
Accelerating optimal approval of priority formulations for antibiotic use in children: meetings report, 7 December 2023 and 19-20 March 2024

20 November 2024
 | Meeting report
Download (1.9 MB)

Overview

On 24 March 2023, WHO launched the first-ever list of priority paediatric formulations for antibiotics, addressing critical gaps in age-appropriate treatments for infants and children. This list, developed through WHO’s Paediatric Drug Optimization (PADO) process, identifies antibiotics urgently needing development to treat infections from high-priority pathogens. WHO, leveraging GAP-f and partners like GARDP and PENTA, led a technical consultation that concluded in March 2024 to review regulatory frameworks and streamline clinical research, aiming to accelerate regulatory approvals and ensure equitable access to effective treatments. The outcomes of this meeting are captured in this report, underscoring the collaborative efforts needed to advance essential paediatric formulations, minimize delays, and support globally aligned, evidence-based care for serious infections in children.

title: Quality criteria for integrating health into Nationally Determined Contributions (‎NDCs)‎

content.body_text: Quality criteria for integrating health into Nationally Determined Contributions (‎NDCs)‎ 19 November 2024 | Publication Download (1.3 MB) Overview This document seeks to guide policy-makers, ministry of health staff, and staff of other government departments leading and contributing to NDCs to integrate health in their countries’ NDCs. It aims to support the health sector to understand the international and national climate plan processes, plans and terminology and the key entry points for health. The document provides an overview of the structure, quality criteria for health integration, examples, and useful resources for the main components of NDCs: leadership and enabling environment; national circumstances and policy priorities; mitigation; adaptation; loss and damage; finance; and implementation. The aim of the document is to provide overarching guidance to national governments to raise the quality and ambition of NDCs, which can be adapted and modified according to the local context and priorities. The quality criteria are not intended to be prescriptive. The overall objective of promoting healthy NDCs is to address the health impacts of climate change, support climate-resilient and low-carbon sustainable health systems, and identify and maximize the health-related co-benefits of climate policies and plans across all relevant sectors. language_versions.title: Critères de qualité applicables à l’intégration de la santé dans les contributions déterminées au niveau national (CDN)
language_versions.body_text: Critères de qualité applicables à l’intégration de la santé dans les contributions déterminées au niveau national (CDN) 19 novembre 2024 | Publication Télécharger (1,1 MB) Vue d’ensemble Le présent document vise à aider les responsables de l’élaboration des politiques, le personnel des ministères de la santé et le personnel d’autres institutions publiques qui dirigent l’élaboration des CDN ou y contribuent à intégrer la santé dans les CDN de leur pays. Il vise également à aider le secteur de la santé à cerner les processus, les stratégies et la terminologie propres aux plans d’action climatique internationaux et nationaux, ainsi que les principaux points d’ancrage en matière de santé. En outre, le présent document donne un aperçu de la structure des CDN et des critères de qualité applicables à l’intégration de la santé dans les CDN, avec à l’appui des exemples et des ressources utiles se rapportant aux principales composantes des CDN, à savoir : l’esprit d’initiative et un environnement favorable ; la situation nationale et les priorités stratégiques ; l’atténuation ; l’adaptation ; les pertes et préjudices ; les finances ; la mise en œuvre. L’objectif du présent document est de fournir aux autorités nationales des orientations globales leur permettant d’améliorer la qualité et le niveau d’ambition des CDN, lesquelles peuvent être adaptées et modifiées selon le contexte et les priorités locales. Les critères de qualité n’ont pas vocation à être prescriptifs. L’objectif global, à savoir la promotion de CDN saines, est de s’attaquer aux effets des changements climatiques sur la santé, de soutenir des systèmes de santé durables, résilients face aux changements climatiques et à faibles émissions de carbone, et de recenser et de maximiser les retombées positives sur la santé des politiques et des plans d’action climatique dans tous les secteurs concernés. language_versions.title: Criterios de calidad para la integración de la salud en las contribuciones determinadas a nivel nacional (‎CDN)‎
language_versions.body_text: Criterios de calidad para la integración de la salud en las contribuciones determinadas a nivel nacional (‎CDN)‎ 19 de noviembre de 2024 | Publicación Descargar (1 MB) Visión de conjunto El presente documento pretende orientar a los responsables de la formulación de políticas, al personal de los ministerios de salud y al personal de otros departamentos gubernamentales que lideran las CDN y contribuyen a ellas con el fin de que integren la salud en las CDN de sus países. Su objetivo es apoyar al sector de la salud para que comprenda la terminología, los planes y los procesos internacionales y nacionales relacionados con el clima, así como los puntos de entrada clave para la salud. El presente documento ofrece una visión general de la estructura, criterios de calidad para la integración de la salud, ejemplos y recursos útiles para los componentes principales de las CDN: liderazgo y entorno propicio; circunstancias nacionales y prioridades en materia de políticas; mitigación; adaptación; pérdidas y daños; finanzas; y aplicación. El objetivo del documento es proporcionar una orientación general a los gobiernos nacionales para elevar la calidad y la ambición de las CDN, que pueden adaptarse y modificarse de acuerdo con el contexto y las prioridades locales. Los criterios de calidad no pretenden ser prescriptivos. El objetivo general de promover CDN para la salud es abordar los efectos del cambio climático en la salud, apoyar los sistemas de salud sostenibles, resilientes al clima y con bajas emisiones de carbono, y determinar y potenciar al máximo los beneficios secundarios relacionados con la salud de las políticas y planes climáticos en todos los sectores pertinentes. Criterios de calidad para la integración de la salud en las contribuciones determinadas a nivel nacional (‎CDN)‎

19 de noviembre de 2024

Visión de conjunto

El presente documento pretende orientar a los responsables de la formulación de políticas, al personal de los ministerios de salud y al personal de otros departamentos gubernamentales que lideran las CDN y contribuyen a ellas con el fin de que integren la salud en las CDN de sus países. Su objetivo es apoyar al sector de la salud para que comprenda la terminología, los planes y los procesos internacionales y nacionales relacionados con el clima, así como los puntos de entrada clave para la salud.

El presente documento ofrece una visión general de la estructura, criterios de calidad para la integración de la salud, ejemplos y recursos útiles para los componentes principales de las CDN: liderazgo y entorno propicio; circunstancias nacionales y prioridades en materia de políticas; mitigación; adaptación; pérdidas y daños; finanzas; y aplicación.

El objetivo del documento es proporcionar una orientación general a los gobiernos nacionales para elevar la calidad y la ambición de las CDN, que pueden adaptarse y modificarse de acuerdo con el contexto y las prioridades locales. Los criterios de calidad no pretenden ser prescriptivos. El objetivo general de promover CDN para la salud es abordar los efectos del cambio climático en la salud, apoyar los sistemas de salud sostenibles, resilientes al clima y con bajas emisiones de carbono, y determinar y potenciar al máximo los beneficios secundarios relacionados con la salud de las políticas y planes climáticos en todos los sectores pertinentes.

title: Facilitation manual: psychological first aid during Ebola virus disease outbreaks, 2nd edition

content.body_text: Facilitation manual: psychological first aid during Ebola virus disease outbreaks, 2nd edition 19 November 2024 | Guideline Download (10.6 MB) Overview This manual is designed to orient helpers to offer psychological first aid (PFA) to people affected by an Ebola outbreak. PFA involves humane, supportive and practical assistance for people who are distressed, in ways that respect their dignity, culture and abilities. This facilitator’s manual is to be used together with the guide Psychological first aid during Ebola virus disease outbreaks. This document was provisionally made available in 2014 and this updated 2024 version is published to ensure that all facts on Ebola virus disease (EVD) are in line with the latest evidence. The review and update of the facts (reflected in the Introduction of this document) was initiated in 2024 by WHO staffand consultants working in both the WHO Department of Mental Health, Brain Health and Substance Use and the WHO Health Emergencies Programme. The 2014 document was searched to identify any instructions or information related to EVD. Any content related to EVD including prevention and control, diagnosis, and treatment in the 2014 version was identified and tabulated for review by the WHO technical leads with expertise in the matter. Based on these inputs, content was then updated. Remaining content in the guide related to training on and provision of psychological first aid was not altered. content.body_text: Annual South-East Asia regional meeting on Operational Planning for Implementation of the Global Influenza Strategy and preparedness for other respiratory viruses in 2025 Meeting report, 19 November 2024, Manila, Philippines 19 November 2024 | Report Download (3.7 MB) Overview The WHO Regional Offices for South-East Asia and the Western Pacific alternately host the annual bi-regional meeting of national influenza centres and influenza surveillance. The South-East Asia Regional Annual Meeting on operational planning for influenza and other respiratory pathogens is held separately a day before the bi-regional meeting. In 2025, this meeting took place in Manila, Philippines, on 19 November. It served as a platform for Member States to discuss priority activities related to the Global Influenza Strategy and other key WHO initiatives, as well as to conduct operational planning for the forthcoming year. The meeting was attended by representatives from Member States of the SE Asia Region and the Regional and country offices. Discussions focused on implementation updates from 2024 in programmatic, surveillance and laboratory areas. Participants collectively defined WHO’s operational priorities in programmatic and laboratory areas related to influenza and other respiratory pathogens. This report presents the proceedings and the operational priorities identified for 2025 WHO Team SEARO Regional Office for the South East Asia (RGO) Number of pages 23 Reference numbers WHO Reference Number: SEA-WHE-24 Copyright

content.body_text: Health labour market analysis for the state of Gujarat 19 November 2024 | Country report Download (7.4 MB) Overview The health labour market analysis (HLMA) in Gujarat explored critical issues within the public health system, including the effectiveness of primary health care service delivery, with a focus on human resource management practices and public-private sector collaboration. The study also examined the secondary level care continuum, emphasizing the role of multi-disciplinary teams and the availability of specialists. As a core component of the HLMA, situational analysis of the health workforce in the state was undertaken, utilizing publicly available data to identify key gaps and inform policy recommendations. title: Health labour market analysis for Assam

content.body_text: Health labour market analysis for Assam 19 November 2024 | Country report Download (5.8 MB) Overview The health labour market analysis (HLMA) for Assam focuses on assessing the distribution, competencies, and gaps within the public health workforce. It provides a situational analysis of health & care workforce to meet the population’s needs, particularly in primary health care, with a focus on maternal and child health services. The analysis also explores current practices aimed at improving access to healthcare, including referral systems and emergency care, especially in hard-to-reach areas. The findings provide insights into workforce challenges to inform strategies to optimize service delivery and address health inequities across the state. title: Birth defects surveillance training: facilitator’s guide, second edition

content.body_text: Birth defects surveillance training: facilitator’s guide, second edition 18 November 2024 | Manual Download (5.9 MB) Overview This Birth Defect Surveillance facilitator (train-the-trainer) guide 2nd edition covers foundational skills needed to begin the development, implementation and ongoing improvement of a congenital anomaly surveillance programme, whether population-based or hospital-based, in particular for countries with limited resources. The congenital anomalies used as examples throughout this course are typically severe, identifiable at birth, and of significant clinical and public health impact. For several, effective primary prevention strategies are available. The course was developed and refined with input from trainers and trainees from more than 15 countries. Clinical case scenarios are added to integrate the discussion of ascertainment and diagnosis with that of primary prevention and data quality improvement. The accompanying materials include: Birth defects surveillance training: facilitator’s guide: participant workbook, 2nd Edition The Birth defects surveillance: A manual for programme managers, 2nd Edition Power point slides: Modules 1 to 3 , Modules 4 to 7 Supplementary materials for local facilitators, can be downloaded from the ICBDSR website: http://www.icbdsr.org/resources/ Birth defects surveillance: quick reference handbook of selected congenital anomalies and infections WHO Team Epidemiology, Monitoring and Evaluation UHL (EME), Maternal, Newborn, Child & Adolescent Health & Ageing (MCA) , Newborn Health (NBH) Editors WHO, CDC, International Clearinghouse for Birth Defects Number of pages 219 Reference numbers ISBN: 9789240098282 Copyright

Overview

This Birth Defect Surveillance facilitator (train-the-trainer) guide 2nd edition covers foundational skills needed to begin the development, implementation and ongoing improvement of a congenital anomaly surveillance programme, whether population-based or hospital-based, in particular for countries with limited resources.

The congenital anomalies used as examples throughout this course are typically severe, identifiable at birth, and of significant clinical and public health impact. For several, effective primary prevention strategies are available.

The course was developed and refined with input from trainers and trainees from more than 15 countries. Clinical case scenarios are added to integrate the discussion of ascertainment and diagnosis with that of primary prevention and data quality improvement.

The congenital anomalies used as examples throughout this course are typically severe, identifiable at birth, and of significant clinical and public health impact. For several, effective primary prevention strategies are available. The course was developed and refined with input from trainers and trainees from more than 15 countries. Clinical case scenarios are added to integrate the discussion of ascertainment and diagnosis with that of primary prevention and data quality improvement. title: The Global Diabetes Compact: progress in supporting its workstreams: technical report

content.body_text: The Global Diabetes Compact: progress in supporting its workstreams: technical report 18 November 2024 | Technical document Download (1 MB) Overview In 2021, WHO launched the Global Diabetes Compact (GDC), an initiative to reduce the risk of diabetes and ensure that all people who are diagnosed with diabetes have access to equitable, comprehensive, affordable and quality treatment and care. The GDC operates through 6 workstreams: 1) access to essential diabetes medicines and health technologies; 2) technical products; 3) prevention, health promotion, and health literacy; 4) country support; 5) research and innovation; and 6) governance. This report provides an update on the technical work undertaken within the second workstream of GDC and presents a list of priority research topics for diabetes. Additionally, the report highlights key areas to address in order to facilitate the translation of research results into policy and practice. title: WHO training package on environmental cleaning: evaluation methodology guide

content.body_text: WHO training package on environmental cleaning: evaluation methodology guide 18 November 2024 | Publication Download (2.1 MB) Overview This guide provides a framework for evaluating the WHO training package, Environmental cleaning and infection prevention and control in health-care facilities in low- and middle-income countries . This training package was designed to improve the competencies of healthcare facility cleaners through a practical, adult-learning approach. By focusing on both process and impact evaluation, this guide aims to provide robust and actionable insights for future implementations and adaptations of the training package. Key considerations include examining the delivery of the intervention, assessing its final outcomes and effects, and utilizing mixed methods (qualitative, quantitative, and microbiological) to capture the multifaceted nature of the training package as a complex intervention. The intended audience for this guide is primarily those tasked with designing and delivering a process and/or impact evaluation, whether in the context of a research study or a type of programme audit. content.body_text: WHO Technical Advisory Group on the responsible use of the life sciences and dual-use research: report of the meeting, 25 June 2024 17 November 2024 | Meeting report Download (915.5 kB) Overview The World Health Organization (WHO) Technical Advisory Group on the Responsible Use of the Life Sciences and Dual-Use Research (TAG-RULS DUR) (1) was established to provide independent advice to WHO on the monitoring and mitigation of biorisks, the advances in the life sciences and related technologies, the governance of dual-use research and the responsible use of the life sciences. This meeting was the second virtual meeting and third overall meeting of 2024. Over the course of the meeting, participants discussed and provided feedback on the first draft of the BioRisk Implementation and Evaluation Framework (BRIEF) Tool, were briefed on the draft WHO course on Dual-Use Research and the Responsible Use of the Life Sciences and delivered updates on activities of the TAG’s four working groups. The TAG-RULS DUR and its working groups will continue to undertake activities on the key topics identified. The group agreed that its next meeting will be held in October 2024. content.body_text: Urban health capacities assessment and response: building a healthy community through healthy food, Gwangju Dong-Gu, Republic of Korea 15 November 2024 | Publication Download (407.9 kB) Overview Assessing and using capacities that create synergies across sectors and levels of governance can significantly improve urban health and well-being. The Urban health capacities assessment and response resource kit comprises a Primer and an accompanying Action Guide which describe these capacities in detail a provide a step-by-step process for facilitators implementing capacity assessments with stakeholders involved with urban health. Training videos show them being used. The Resource Kit also comprises a series of City examples, which illustrate the breadth of urban health goals that have already been used to improve urban health goals. They describe the practical experiences of particular cities that have used these tools to support their efforts to improve urban health. This City example describes how a multisectoral team in Gwangju Dong-Gu, Republic of Korea, used the Resource Kit to support work to build a healthy community through healthy food. title: Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control: Framework, indicators and application

content.body_text: Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control: Framework, indicators and application 14 November 2024 | Guidance (normative) Download (1.1 MB) Overview The Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control by WHO provides a comprehensive framework to support countries in tracking and managing diabetes prevention, care, and outcomes. This document outlines indicators across 4 domains: health system determinants, service delivery, risk factors, and outcomes/impacts. The guidance helps countries align their monitoring efforts with WHO’s global diabetes targets, Global Diabetes Compact, and relevant global NCD targets. It emphasizes the importance of collecting, analysing, and utilizing data to inform policy and resource allocation. Specific indicators measure aspects like access to essential medications, prevalence of key risk factors, and control of blood glucose and blood pressure. Each indicator includes detailed metadata, which outlines definitions, data sources, and methods of estimation, ensuring standardized data collection and reliable comparisons across countries. Through structured monitoring, the framework aids countries in evaluating their diabetes interventions, identifying gaps, and prioritizing resources. Additionally, the guidance supports countries in meeting the sustainable development goals related to reducing noncommunicable diseases and improving universal health coverage. The guidance encourages adaptation to national contexts, emphasizing the integration of innovative data collection methods and digital technologies to improve data quality and accessibility. title: Sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health: report on the 2023 policy survey

content.body_text: Sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health: report on the 2023 policy survey 12 November 2024 | Global report Download (2.5 MB) Overview Evidence- and rights-based national policies, guidelines and legislation play a key role in improving sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health (SRMNCAH), framing the enabling environment for equitable provision and accessibility of quality services. The SRMNCAH policy survey monitors the existence of national SRMNCAH laws, policies, strategies and guidelines and the extent to which they are aligned with WHO recommendations on SRMNCAH. This publication reports on the findings from the 2023 WHO SRMNCAH policy survey. In the 2023 survey, which was completed by SRMNCAH focal points in each country’s ministry of health with support from WHO country offices and other national stakeholders, respondents completed modules on: (i) cross-cutting issues related to SRMNCAH; (ii) maternal and newborn health; (iii) child health; (iv) adolescent health; (v) sexual and reproductive health; and (vi) violence against women. The questionnaire was completed through a web-based platform that allows countries to submit national source documents (e.g., laws, policies, strategic plans, and guidelines) that were used to respond the survey. These documents are available through a searchable repository . An online data visualization tool for the 2023 SRMNCAH policy survey can be accessed here . Regional Strategic Roadmap for enhancing research and innovation towards ending tuberculosis in the WHO South-East Asia Region: 2024–2026., 2024

12 November 2024
 | Publication
Download (1.5 MB)

Overview

Globally, tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality. It was the second largest killer among infectious diseases in 2022. Despite being a curable and preventable disease, TB extracts an enormous human and societal toll. All Member States have committed to end TB by 2030, as part of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs). The corresponding End TB targets are 80% reduction in TB incidence rate and 90% reduction in the number of TB deaths, relative to 2015 and elimination of catastrophic costs due to the disease for affected families.

Ending TB requires a comprehensive strategy integrating medical, public health and social interventions, focused on the prevention, early diagnosis and treatment of TB, while ensuring patient support during the process. WHO has formulated and keeps updating guidelines on various interventions required to implement the End TB Strategy, including those for medical approaches and for reduction of the TB burden, based on the available scientific evidence.  Several stakeholders are playing a pivotal role in implementing these guidelines and ensuring equitable access to prevention, diagnosis and treatment services for those affected by TB. Despite significant efforts, global progress towards ending TB has been slow due to insufficient resources, suboptimal tools, inadequate access to the services, lack of multisectoral action and inadequate attention to the  socioeconomic determinants of TB. Globally, an estimated US$ 22 billion per year is needed to finance the TB response. As of 2022, only US$ 5.8 billion was available, with US$ 1.1 billion of this coming from international donor funding. Progress received a further setback due to disruptions in TB services during the COVID-19 pandemic. At the current rate of progress, the target of reducing the global burden by 2030 as envisioned in the SDGs is unlikely to be met.  

Political commitment to end TB has steadily increased, as highlighted by the declarations in the second United Nations High-Level Meeting on the fight against TB, held in September 2023 at New York, and the South-East Asian Regional High-Level meetings. The most recent regional meeting was held in 2023 at Gandhinagar, Gujarat, which led to the Gandhinagar Declaration. These commitments stem from the recognition that TB remains one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases, disproportionately affecting the poorest and most vulnerable populations.

“Research and innovation” is one of the three core pillars of the WHO End TB Strategy and is highly relevant for accelerating progress towards ending TB by understanding the epidemiology of TB better, developing new tools for prevention, diagnosis and treatment, and for optimal utilization of existing tools and resources. The United Nations High-Level meetings on TB in 2018 and 2023 have also endorsed the importance of research and innovation, reiterating the need for increased funding for TB research.

title: Diagnostic testing and testing strategies for mpox: interim guidance, 12 November 2024

content.body_text: Diagnostic testing and testing strategies for mpox: interim guidance, 12 November 2024 12 November 2024 | Technical document Download (688.5 kB) Overview This is the fourth updated version of the interim guidance on Diagnostic testing for the monkeypox virus and supersedes the previous guidance published on 10 May 2024. This version includes references and conclusions drawn from the most recent data and evidence available on diagnostic performance for various testing methods, including near-patient POC testing options, which, based on the available evidence, can be considered in diagnostics decentralization strategies. It also reviewed recent evidence on performance of antigen RDT and confirmed the recommendation against their use provided in previous versions. It further highlights key considerations for diagnostic and testing strategies that may be used in at different epidemiological phases of an outbreak, and recommendations on avoiding gene target failures and differentiating MPXV clades. Finally, it also reports a change in the recommendation for transport from Category A to Category B for diagnostic samples containing MPXV (while virus isolates are still required to be shipped as Category A). Previous Versions: Laboratory testing for the monkeypox virus: interim guidance, 23 May 2022 Diagnostic testing for the monkeypox virus (MPXV): Interim Guidance, 09 November 2023 Diagnostic testing for the monkeypox virus (MPXV): interim guidance, 10 May 2024 Related: Integration of HIV and syphilis testing services as part of mpox response: standard operating procedures Target product profiles for tests used for mpox (‎monkeypox)‎ diagnosis WHO Team Emergency Operations (EMO), Emerging Diseases and Zoonoses (EZD), Public Health Laboratory Strengthening (PHL) Editors World Health Organization Number of pages 28 Reference numbers WHO Reference Number: B09166 Copyright
content.body_html:
Diagnostic testing and testing strategies for mpox: interim guidance, 12 November 2024

12 November 2024
 | Technical document
Download (688.5 kB)

Overview

This is the fourth updated version of the interim guidance on Diagnostic testing for the monkeypox virus and
supersedes the previous guidance published on 10 May 2024. This version includes references and conclusions 
drawn from the most recent data and evidence available on diagnostic performance for various testing methods, 
including near-patient POC testing options, which, based on the available evidence, can be considered in diagnostics decentralization strategies. It also reviewed recent evidence on performance of antigen RDT and confirmed the recommendation against their use provided in previous versions. It further highlights key considerations for diagnostic and testing strategies that may be used in at different epidemiological phases of an outbreak, and recommendations on avoiding gene target failures and differentiating MPXV clades. Finally, it also reports a change in the recommendation for transport from Category A to Category B for diagnostic samples containing MPXV (while virus isolates are still required to be shipped as Category A).

title: Quality control of SHA-based health accounts data

content.body_text: Quality control of SHA-based health accounts data 11 November 2024 | Technical document Download (3.5 MB) Overview The document provides a comprehensive set of instructions on what to check and how to check the health expenditure data that are produced with health accounts using the SHA2011 framework. The quality control process includes verifying the mapping of the health expenditure under the classifications, HF, FS, HC, HP, DIS, AGE, etc., basic accounting rules in the reported data, and consistency. The document serves as a reference for the target audience - data producers and data users. It will help data producers, including the country health accounts team and the WHO headquarters team, to improve the quality of health expenditure data production, while it will also help data users to understand the data production process and methodology. language_versions.title: Contrôle de la qualité des données relatives au système decomptes de la santé
language_versions.body_text: Contrôle de la qualité des données relatives au système decomptes de la santé 11 novembre 2024 | Rapport technique Télécharger (2,6 MB) Vue d’ensemble Le document fournit un ensemble complet d'instructions sur ce qu'il faut vérifier et comment vérifier les données sur les dépenses de santé qui sont produites en utilisant le cadre des comptes de la santé (SCS2011). Le processus de contrôle de la qualité comprend la vérification de la cartographie des dépenses de santé sous les classifications HF, FS, HC, HP, DIS, AGE, etc., des règles comptables de base (absence de données négatives, dépense égale à la somme des parties etc), et de la cohérence des données rapportées. Le document sert de référence au public cible - producteurs et utilisateurs de données. Il aidera les producteurs de données, y compris les équipes pays des comptes de la santé et l'équipe du siège de l'OMS, à améliorer la qualité des données de dépenses de santé produites, tout en aidant également les utilisateurs de données à comprendre le processus de production des données et la méthodologie sous-jacente. title: List of key WHO-recommended maternal and newborn health commodities

content.body_text: List of key WHO-recommended maternal and newborn health commodities 10 November 2024 | Guidance (normative) Download (1.3 MB) Overview This document provides a list of key WHO-recommended maternal and newborn health commodities and aims to accelerate progress towards the SDGs. It consolidates the key and enabling commodities from existing WHO guidelines on maternal and newborn health. The commodities included in the list are either critical for reducing maternal, fetal, and/or newborn deaths, or are essential for providing high-quality care. Consumables and training materials are excluded. The list was produced by WHO’s Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA), in collaboration with WHO technical departments and the WHO Strategic and Technical Advisory Group of Experts for Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (STAGE). 10 November 2024
 | Guidance (normative)
Download (1.3 MB)

Overview

This document provides a list of key WHO-recommended maternal and newborn health commodities and aims to accelerate progress towards the SDGs. It consolidates the key and enabling commodities from existing WHO guidelines on maternal and newborn health.

The commodities included in the list are either critical for reducing maternal, fetal, and/or newborn deaths, or are essential for providing high-quality care. Consumables and training materials are excluded.

The list was produced by WHO’s Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA), in collaboration with WHO technical departments and the WHO Strategic and Technical Advisory Group of Experts for Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (STAGE).

content.body_text: Joint external evaluation of the International Health Regulations (‎2005)‎ core capacities of Indonesia Mission report, 16-20 October 2023 8 November 2024 | Country report Download (2.5 MB) Overview The Joint External Evaluation (JEE) team would like to express its appreciation to Indonesia for volunteering for a second round of JEE. This demonstrates commitment, foresight, and leadership from the highest levels of government, crucial for long-term success in building and sustaining Indonesia’s core capacities under the International Health Regulations (2005) (IHR). The external team commends Indonesia for enhancing health security by implementing IHR through committed leadership, which is of significant importance not just regionally, but also globally. As a large country spread over 17 000 islands, Indonesia’s size, population, and vulnerability to natural disasters, along with its social, economic, and administrative diversity, pose unique challenges to public health. The country has robustly responded to these challenges, taking public health leadership roles both regionally and globally. Globally, Indonesia held the Global Health Security Agenda (GHSA) steering group chair in 2016, co-leads the Global Health Security Agenda (GHSA) Zoonotic Diseases Action Package, and is a member of the Global Health Security Agenda (GHSA) Steering Group. Indonesia assumed the G20 presidency in 2022, and during its tenure, the Pandemic Fund was launched to enhance capacities for pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response at national, regional, and global levels. Additionally, as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) chair in 2023, Indonesia saw the adoption of the ASEAN Leaders' Declaration on the One Health Initiative, marking a significant milestone in efforts to establish a more resilient health security architecture in the region. The JEE process is particularly important for a nation facing a complex array of challenges, offering an opportunity for Indonesia to identify strengths, address challenges, and demonstrate further leadership in strengthening health security. Indonesia’s geographically disparate territory necessitates high-level national coordination and monitoring to ensure progress in national core capacities under the IHR (2005), as demonstrated by the findings of Indonesia’s JEE self-assessment exercise conducted by the Government of Indonesia and supported by Indonesian experts and confirmed by their joint work with the JEE external experts’ team during the evaluation week. The JEE tool is currently in its third iteration (Version 3.0) and was updated most recently with the lessons and experiences shared by countries and technical partners in 2022 (in line with the IHR Review Committee and Independent Oversight and Advisory Committee recommendations). Indonesia last completed the JEE in 2017 using Version 1 of the tool. The significant improvements to the tool over the past five years mean that comparison of progress using just the scores generated through these evaluations is both invalid and contraindicated. Critical consideration of the achievements to date and the advancement needed, by comparing the qualitative results of the evaluations, highlighting the strengths and best practices, gaps and challenges and the priority actions identified through consensus are of utmost importance. Through the rich engagement between the internal and external experts afforded by this comprehensive evaluation, five overarching cross-cutting recommendations emerged. These are intended to effectively leverage the broad health systems transformation initiatives that are ongoing and address the interlinked challenges affecting Indonesia’s capacities in several technical areas, as discussed in detail below. Overview

The Joint External Evaluation (JEE) team would like to express its appreciation to Indonesia for volunteering for a second round of JEE. This demonstrates commitment, foresight, and leadership from the highest levels of government, crucial for long-term success in building and sustaining Indonesia’s core capacities under the International Health Regulations (2005) (IHR). The external team commends Indonesia for enhancing health security by implementing IHR through committed leadership, which is of significant importance not just regionally, but also globally. As a large country spread over 17 000 islands, Indonesia’s size, population, and vulnerability to natural disasters, along with its social, economic, and administrative diversity, pose unique challenges to public health. The country has robustly responded to these challenges, taking public health leadership roles both regionally and globally.

Globally, Indonesia held the Global Health Security Agenda (GHSA) steering group chair in 2016, co-leads the Global Health Security Agenda (GHSA) Zoonotic Diseases Action Package, and is a member of the Global Health Security Agenda (GHSA) Steering Group. Indonesia assumed the G20 presidency in 2022, and during its tenure, the Pandemic Fund was launched to enhance capacities for pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response at national, regional, and global levels. Additionally, as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) chair in 2023, Indonesia saw the adoption of the ASEAN Leaders' Declaration on the One Health Initiative, marking a significant milestone in efforts to establish a more resilient health security architecture in the region. The JEE process is particularly important for a nation facing a complex array of challenges, offering an opportunity for Indonesia to identify strengths, address challenges, and demonstrate further leadership in strengthening health security. Indonesia’s geographically disparate territory necessitates high-level national coordination and monitoring to ensure progress in national core capacities under the IHR (2005), as demonstrated by the findings of Indonesia’s JEE self-assessment exercise conducted by the Government of Indonesia and supported by Indonesian experts and confirmed by their joint work with the JEE external experts’ team during the evaluation week.

The JEE tool is currently in its third iteration (Version 3.0) and was updated most recently with the lessons and experiences shared by countries and technical partners in 2022 (in line with the IHR Review Committee and Independent Oversight and Advisory Committee recommendations). Indonesia last completed the JEE in 2017 using Version 1 of the tool. The significant improvements to the tool over the past five years mean that comparison of progress using just the scores generated through these evaluations is both invalid and contraindicated. Critical consideration of the achievements to date and the advancement needed, by comparing the qualitative results of the evaluations, highlighting the strengths and best practices, gaps and challenges and the priority actions identified through consensus are of utmost importance.

Through the rich engagement between the internal and external experts afforded by this comprehensive evaluation, five overarching cross-cutting recommendations emerged. These are intended to effectively leverage the broad health systems transformation initiatives that are ongoing and address the interlinked challenges affecting Indonesia’s capacities in several technical areas, as discussed in detail below.
